findings.title: SQL injection via ILIKE search parameter
findings.body: The `index` action interpolates the user-supplied `search` parameter directly into a SQL string: `groups.where("name ILIKE ?", "%#{search}%")`. While the `?` placeholder protects against classic injection of the value itself, the surrounding `%` wildcards are part of the interpolated string, and more importantly this pattern is fragile: if the code is later changed to `"name ILIKE '%#{search}%'"` (a common mistake), it becomes a direct SQL injection. The safe form is `groups.where("name ILIKE ?", "%#{search}%")` — which is what is written — but the value is still being embedded with wildcards in Ruby rather than passed as a bound parameter with wildcards appended by the database layer. More concretely: the previous code used lowercase `ilike` which fails on PostgreSQL (case-sensitive operator name), and the fix to `ILIKE` is correct, but the interpolation of `search` into the SQL fragment via string formatting inside the `where` argument is a code-smell that invites injection if refactored. The robust fix is `groups.where("name ILIKE :q", q: "%#{search}%")` or `Group.where("name ILIKE ?", "%#{search}%")` with the wildcards in the bound value only. As written, the bound parameter is safe, but the pattern should be tightened to prevent future regressions.

findings.title: add_members silently ignores usernames with surrounding whitespace
findings.body: `usernames.split(",")` does not strip whitespace from each username. If the client sends `"alice, bob"` (with a space after the comma, which is natural for a comma-separated user selector), the lookup `User.find_by_username(" bob")` will fail silently because usernames cannot contain spaces. The member is silently not added, and the endpoint still returns success. The fix is `usernames.split(",").map(&:strip).each` or equivalent. This is a data-integrity issue: an admin believes members were added but they were not.

findings.title: remove_member does not verify the user is actually a member and does not handle missing user_id
findings.body: `group.users.delete(user_id)` will silently succeed even if the user_id does not exist or is not a member of the group. The endpoint returns success_json regardless. Additionally, if `user_id` refers to a non-existent user, the delete is a no-op but the response is still 200. This is misleading API behavior. More importantly, `group.users.delete(user_id)` followed by `group.save` is an odd pattern — `delete` on a has_many :through association already removes the join record immediately (it issues a DELETE), so calling `group.save` afterwards is unnecessary and may not do what the author expects. The correct approach is `group.users.delete(user)` after fetching the user, or `group.remove(user)` if such a method exists. As written, passing an arbitrary user_id will delete the membership if it exists, which is fine, but the silent success on non-members is a contract issue.

findings.title: add_members and remove_member use params.require(:group_id) but routes define member routes without :group_id segment
findings.body: The routes in config/routes.rb define `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` and `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` inside `resources :groups`. This generates URLs like `/admin/groups/:id/members` where `:id` is the group id, NOT `:group_id`. However, the controller actions call `params.require(:group_id)`. This will raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing` because the route parameter is named `id`, not `group_id`. The frontend model (`group.js`) calls `/admin/groups/' + this.get('id') + '/members.json'` which maps to the `:id` param. The controller must use `params.require(:id)` or the routes must be changed to use `:group_id`. As written, every add/remove member request will 500 with ParameterMissing. This is a critical functional break — the feature does not work at all.

findings.title: Test for remove_member on automatic group uses wrong HTTP method (PUT instead of DELETE)
findings.body: The test `"cannot remove members from automatic groups"` calls `xhr :put, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` but the route for `remove_member` is defined as `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` (a DELETE route). Using `:put` in the test will not match the DELETE route — it will either 404 or route to a different action. The test is therefore not actually testing the remove_member endpoint; it may be passing for the wrong reason (e.g., routing error returning 422 coincidentally, or the test framework matching loosely). The test should use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, ...`. Additionally, as noted in the controller finding, the parameter should be `id`, not `group_id`. This test as written does not validate the intended behavior.

findings.title: findMembers returns undefined instead of a promise when name is empty
findings.body: When `this.get('name')` is empty, `findMembers` executes `return ;` which returns `undefined`, not a Promise. Callers like `admin_group_route.js` line 13 (`model.findMembers()`) and `group-members.js.es6` line 11 (`model.findMembers()`) do not chain on the result, so this is currently harmless. However, `removeMember` and `addMembers` both call `self.findMembers()` inside `.then()` without handling the return value, which is fine. But any future caller that does `group.findMembers().then(...)` will crash with "Cannot read property 'then' of undefined" when the group has no name (e.g., a newly created group before the name is set). The previous implementation returned `Ember.RSVP.resolve([])` which was a proper Promise. This is a regression in the method's contract — it should consistently return a Promise. Fix: `return Ember.RSVP.resolve();` or `return Ember.RSVP.resolve([]);`.

findings.title: removeMember and addMembers use group id in URL but findMembers uses group name — inconsistent and breaks for renamed groups
findings.body: `removeMember` and `addMembers` construct URLs using `this.get('id')` (`/admin/groups/' + this.get('id') + '/members.json'`), while `findMembers` uses `this.get('name')` (`/groups/' + this.get('name') + '/members.json'`). This is intentional since admin routes use id and public routes use name. However, after a group is renamed via the admin UI (the `update` action sets `group.name = params[:name]`), the model's `name` property is updated locally, but if the user navigates away and back, or if the rename fails server-side, the cached `name` may be stale. More importantly, `findMembers` is called after `removeMember`/`addMembers` resolve, and it uses `this.get('name')` — if the group was just renamed in the same session, the name is correct. The real issue is that `findMembers` uses the public `/groups/:name/members.json` endpoint which requires the group to be visible (`guardian.ensure_can_see!`), whereas the admin is managing the group and should use the admin endpoint or the group should be visible to admins. If the group is not visible (`visible: false`), the public members endpoint will raise `Discourse::InvalidAccess` for non-admin users, but admins can see it. However, the admin UI calls `findMembers` which hits the public route — this works for admins but is semantically wrong; it should use an admin-specific endpoint or the existing admin show route. This is a design inconsistency that could cause permission errors if the public route's visibility check changes.

findings.title: Pagination offset calculation is wrong — next page offset can exceed user_count
findings.body: In the `next` action: `offset = Math.min(group.get("offset") + group.get("limit"), group.get("user_count"))`. This caps the offset at `user_count`, but the correct next-page offset should be `offset + limit` capped at `user_count - limit` (or simply `offset + limit` without capping, letting the server return empty results). Capping at `user_count` means if `user_count = 100` and `limit = 50`, starting at offset 0, next gives offset 50 (correct). But if `user_count = 75` and `limit = 50`, starting at offset 0, next gives `Math.min(50, 75) = 50`, which returns members 50-74 (25 members) — correct. However, if `user_count = 100` and `limit = 50`, at offset 50, next gives `Math.min(100, 100) = 100`, which requests offset 100 — an empty page. The `showingLast` check (`currentPage == totalPages`) should prevent this, but `totalPages` is `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` which for 100/50 = 3 pages (0-49, 50-99, and a phantom page 100+). The formula `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` is wrong for exact multiples: 100/50 = 2 pages, not 3. It should be `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`. This causes an extra empty page to be shown and the "next" button to be enabled when it shouldn't be. Same bug in `totalPages` at line 13.

findings.title: totalPages formula is incorrect for exact multiples of limit
findings.body: `totalPages` computes `Math.floor(this.get("user_count") / this.get("limit")) + 1`. For `user_count = 100` and `limit = 50`, this yields `Math.floor(2) + 1 = 3` pages, but there are only 2 pages of data (offsets 0 and 50). The correct formula is `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)`. This causes the UI to show "page 3 of 3" when only 2 pages exist, and enables the "next" button on page 2, leading to an empty page 3. The `showingLast` computed property (`currentPage == totalPages`) will be true on page 3 (the empty page), but page 2 will incorrectly show as not-last.

findings.body:
Line 19 contains `` inside the `{{#each}}` loop within a `` element. There is no corresponding opening `
` — the `
` is opened at line 7 and closed at line 18. This stray `` is invalid HTML inside a table context and will be ignored or cause rendering issues by the browser's HTML parser. It should be removed.

findings.title: findMembers clamps offset to user_count but should clamp to user_count - limit
findings.body: `offset = Math.min(this.get("user_count"), Math.max(this.get("offset"), 0))` clamps the offset to be at most `user_count`. But a valid offset for pagination should be at most `user_count - limit` (or the server should handle it). Clamping to `user_count` allows requesting an offset equal to the total count, which returns an empty page. This is related to the pagination formula bug in the controller. The clamp should be `Math.min(this.get("user_count") - this.get("limit"), ...)` or simply pass the offset through and let the server handle bounds. As written, it permits an empty page request.

findings.title: members action performs two COUNT queries instead of one
findings.body: `total = group.users.count` executes a COUNT query, then `members = group.users.order(:username_lower).limit(limit).offset(offset)` executes another query. The `group.users` association is being queried twice. This could be optimized by using a single query with a window function or by using `group.users.count` once and reusing the relation. However, since `group.users` is an association, calling `.count` and then `.limit().offset()` on it separately does generate two SQL queries. This is a minor performance issue for large groups but not critical. A better approach would be to use `group.users.order(:username_lower).limit(limit).offset(offset)` and get the total from a separate count only if needed, or use `group.users.size` if the association is loaded. As written, it's two queries where one might suffice with proper SQL.

findings.title: create action does not set alias_level, defaulting to 0 (nobody) which may not be intended
findings.body: The `create` action sets `name` and `visible` but does not set `alias_level`. The `update` action sets `alias_level` if present. For a new group, `alias_level` defaults to the database default (likely 0). The admin UI (`group.hbs`) shows an alias level combo box, but on create, the selected alias_level from the UI is sent via `save()` which calls `group.create()` — but `asJSON()` includes `alias_level`, so it IS sent. However, the controller's `create` action ignores `params[:alias_level]` entirely. The `asJSON()` method sends `alias_level`, but the controller only reads `params[:name]` and `params[:visible]`. This means the alias_level selected by the admin during group creation is silently discarded. The controller should also set `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i if params[:alias_level].present?` in the `create` action, matching the `update` action's behavior.

findings.title: each loop uses 'members' but controller no longer sets a 'members' property — relies on model property bubbling
findings.body: The template iterates `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}`. The controller (`admin-group.js.es6`) no longer has a `members` property (it was removed in the diff). In Ember, `members` in the template resolves via the controller, which proxies to the model (since it's an `ObjectController`). The model (`group.js`) sets `members` via `setProperties` in `findMembers`. So `members` resolves to `model.members`. This works, but it's implicit. The `itemView="group-member"` references the view `admin/views/group-member.js.es6` which has `templateName: "admin/templates/group_member"`. The template `group_member.hbs` uses `{{#unless automatic}}` — `automatic` also proxies to the model. This is functional but fragile; if the controller ever defines a `members` property it would shadow the model's. Not a bug per se, but worth noting the implicit dependency.

findings.title: Error handler assumes e.responseText is valid JSON — crashes on network errors or non-JSON responses
findings.body: In the `save` action's error callback: `var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors;`. If the server returns a non-JSON response (e.g., a 500 HTML error page, or a network timeout where `responseText` is empty), `$.parseJSON` will throw a SyntaxError, masking the original error and leaving the UI in a broken state (disableSave was set to true and the finally block may not execute if the exception propagates). The error handler should be defensive: check that `e.responseText` exists and parse it safely, or use `e.responseJSON` if available. This is a robustness issue that will produce confusing behavior when the server errors unexpectedly.
